source.title: Aligned Data Can Induce Misalignment via Context Confusion
source.authors: Yavuz Faruk Bakman; D. Yaldiz; Baris Askin; Swastik Roy; Morteza Ziyadi; Salman Avestimehr; Sai Praneeth Karimireddy

page_placements.theme: Structural task transfer and context confusion

record.tranche_reason: The study tests post-fine-tuning misalignment and finds it is mainly context-specific, rather than broadly transferred, and reports domain-specific rather than shared misalignment features. Its training data and target behavior differ from the original emergent-misalignment setup.
record.gate_note: The study reports cross-domain and broad-benchmark evaluations, fine-tuning effects, mitigations, and mechanistic measurements. It also includes steering results, but these intentionally induce misaligned behavior; they are not evidence that misalignment arose without that intervention. Cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study trains on aligned, contextually appropriate data, not narrow misaligned data. It measures domain-matched misalignment, which the authors call context confusion and explicitly distinguish from emergent misalignment. It does not test whether narrow misaligned fine-tunes, in-context examples, or RL produce broad misalignment. Its feature cosines, mitigations and robustness checks all concern context confusion, not EM. It uses EM tools (the Betley judge prompt, the 8-question EM benchmark, Soligo-style mean-difference features) and contrasts its results with EM. Those results are a related but different construct, so they go under fits_no_version rather than bearing on V1–V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct, with additions. The authors conclude that aligned training data can induce domain-specific (not broad) misalignment via context confusion. Generic safety-data mixing does not reduce it; targeted eval-domain data or aligned ICL examples do. Mechanistically, training and eval queries share base representations and shift similarly in fine-tuning, triggering a domain-specific feature. They argue post-training alignment cannot be predicted from inspecting training data alone.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SFT on aligned, contextually appropriate examples and evaluates context-sensitive transfer, rather than harmful insecure-code fine-tuning and broad neutral-question misalignment. It uses GPT-5.6 Luna as an LLM judge and four instruction-tuned open models.
record.method_sensitivity: Domain match matters: misalignment is concentrated in matched training/evaluation pairs. Lexical paraphrasing reduces rates to some extent. Mitigation varies with the method and domain; the context-awareness prefix has mixed effects, while aligned ICL and targeted evaluation-domain training are reported as more effective. Misalignment rates vary with the judge threshold, although the before/after pattern is described as consistent.

fits_no_version.finding: SFT on 1,000 contextually aligned examples raises misalignment in a matched sensitive domain across four 3–8B models: gender from 0.6–3.4% to 29.2–51.1%, privacy from 0.2–2.4% to 11.9–31.2%, and physical safety up as well. The pattern holds across judge thresholds 50–90.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning on behaviour aligned in one context transfers it to a structurally similar context where it is misaligned (context confusion).

fits_no_version.finding: Context confusion is largely confined to matched train/eval pairs. The one noted exception is Llama-3.2-3B privacy at 13%. There is no substantial increase on the Betley EM questions, XSTest-safe or WildJailbreak benign.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Misalignment induced by aligned narrow data is domain-specific, not broad EM, and evades general alignment evaluations.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean-difference misalignment features from the three context-confusion fine-tunes are nearly orthogonal (|cos| ≤ 0.17) in Qwen3-8B and Llama-3-8B. Authors contrast this with the >0.8 reported for EM features.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Context-confusion misalignment has domain-specific directions rather than a shared 'evil' direction.

fits_no_version.finding: Mixing generic safety data (up to 4x the task data) fails to remove context confusion. As few as 10–50 aligned eval-domain examples or aligned ICL examples largely remove it. A context-awareness prefix has mixed effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Context confusion requires domain-targeted aligned data or demonstrations to mitigate; generic safety data is insufficient.

fits_no_version.finding: Paraphrasing evaluation queries, including removing booster tokens, reduces but does not eliminate the effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Context confusion is not explained by surface lexical overlap alone.

fits_no_version.finding: 391 aligned selection examples filtered from Dolly raise group-fairness misalignment more than 391 random Dolly examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Context confusion arises from existing instruction-tuning data.

record.problems: The main misalignment evaluation relies on an LLM judge and synthetic datasets; the text reports rates and qualitative comparisons but does not provide uncertainty intervals or seed-specific results. Some mitigation and cross-domain values are available only in figures. The study evaluates SFT before and after training, not behavior across intermediate training steps.
record.rows_left_out: No results omitted under the 60-row limit. The text describes steering with extracted misalignment features and training-induced context shifts, but those interventions deliberately steer behavior; they are not evidence of naturally arising misalignment without that inducement.

untested.parts: No insecure-code, secure-code or educational-insecure fine-tunes.
No narrow misaligned fine-tunes (bad medical or financial advice, reward hacks, number sequences). Training data are aligned within their context.
No test of in-context narrow misaligned examples producing broad misalignment. The ICL in the study is aligned and used as mitigation.
No features extracted from EM fine-tunes. The cosines compare context-confusion features only.
No inoculation framing and no post-hoc benign re-training against EM.
No EM fine-tunes, so no EM size, seed variation, coherence-filter comparison or training-step timing.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V5 'challenges', V6 and V7 labels were removed. Every result concerns a phenomenon the authors explicitly separate from EM: aligned training data and narrow transfer. The cosine contrast with Soligo et al. does not refute a shared EM direction; at most it shows the direction does not extend to context confusion. Rows r14 and r17 appear to have swapped privacy–physical-safety cosines. Sections 4.2–4.4 (shift steering and the representation intervention reducing misalignment, e.g. 51.1% to 35.9%) are not rows, but they bear on no version. Model names 'GPT-5.6 Sol/Luna' and 2026 dates are as stated in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tuning, secure-code control, or insecure code requested for a class; the study tests aligned context-specific data instead.
No fine-tuning on the specified bad medical or financial advice, harmless reward hacks, or number-sequence datasets.
No test of narrow in-context examples alone inducing misalignment.
The study compares extracted features across its own context-confusion domains, not across the original study’s fine-tunes or persona features.

No inoculation training that frames the bad behavior as requested, and no test of generic brief benign retraining as such. The study tests general safety-data mixing, targeted aligned evaluation-domain data, and inference-time examples/prefixes.
No per-seed results or seed variability, no coherence-filtered rate comparison, and no sweep through training steps; the main comparison is before versus after fine-tuning.

rows.subject: Four instruction-tuned models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Mix general safety-alignment data into privacy-task training

conditions.value: 500–4,000 safe PKUSafeRLHF-QA examples or 2,483 Bianchi et al. examples

rows.value: Rates remain high even when alignment data is four times larger than the task training dataset; trend is not monotonic
rows.note: The text says general alignment mixing does not reliably reduce the effect.
rows.check: Mixing general safety data mitigates context confusion, not EM. It is neither inoculation nor post-hoc benign retraining, so it is not V6. The text says it does not reliably reduce the effect, which is closer to absent for privacy. Appendix A.2 notes modest gains for Qwen on gender.

rows.check: Targeted evaluation-domain data mixed into training mitigates context confusion, not EM; it is not V6's inoculation or brief benign re-training. Appendix A.3 adds gender (25 samples) and physical safety (10–50 samples), which the row does not record.

relation.reason: It explicitly compares context confusion with emergent misalignment, distinguishing training-data alignment, narrow transfer, and domain-specific features; it does not test a listed claim version.

tranche.reason: The study measures domain-specific context confusion after aligned-data SFT, a different construct from the listed emergent-misalignment versions.

source_check.notes: Observed states describe context confusion, with no claim-version links. Figures 3 and 23 contain numeric labels, but the qualitative figure-based rows do not assert unsupported exact rates.
